title: Tribes: Ascend
text: A year ago I stood in line for PAX East 2011 and saw a trailer for a game I never thought I'd see. The original Starsiege: Tribes was the first game I ever played online, and I was enthralled by it from my first flag grab. Ascend is very much the inheritor of this classic series' legacy, and though it has modern trappings like regen health and an experience system, these do not greatly detract from the core gameplay.  Ascend is easy to start playing, but is just as skill-intensive as it' forebears. You can't just  "press button, win game."  You have to play hard or go home. Ascend's sprawling levels, varied weapons, blinding speeds, and high-flying acrobatics set it in a class above other shooters, and has a variety of PC-friendly features such as support for custom servers. Noobtube in CoD and collect hats in TF2 if you wish, but when you're ready to quit being a shazbot and play with the big kids, then strap on your jetpack, grab a spinfusor and play Tribes: Ascend.

title: Trine 3: The Artifacts of Power
text: First things first: Trine 3 isn't a terrible game in itself, it's just a really poor entry into the franchise and VASTLY overpriced. I completed the game, as you can see, in about 4 hours. At 22 bucks this is waaaaaay too expensive. In comparison: I invested 14 hours into Trine 2! That is more than triple the amount of play time...and that game was cheaper as well. On to the game itself. You once again guide Pontius, Zoya and Amadeus I think his name is through a series of levels to continue the story for the sake of the story. I can't remember everything, but it seemed Trine 2 had a perfectly fine ending. Well, Trine 3 starts with our heroes being assembled by the Trine...again. After 3 short introductory missions with each hero the real missions start...a whopping 4!!!!! Then you have about 12 very short side missions and 1 boss mission at the end. The only reason the side missions seem to exist is to help you gather enough "Trineangles" to unlock other missions...so, you better grab as many of them as you can, because for the final boss you need 900 of them (I had 975 and missed a few, so there are probably 1,000 in the game). That means you can't even skip the side missions if you wanted to...these by the way always revolve around 1 of our heroes only. At least they explain how and why. Some of them are combat arenas you have to survive. Gameplay: Remember how in Trine 2 you could gather "Trineangles" to improve your skills? Well, skills are gone. Completely. Each character now has about 1 thing they can do and that's it: Pontius is the dedicated fighter, who can smash, stomp, rush and block enemies. He's also the only one who can cut ropes and vines. Amadeus can conjure 1 mechanical box and manipulate certain objects. Zoya...well, she can shoot arrows (which nobody needs) and swing around and tie a rope to certain objects...yay. I think she went from my most played character to my least played one. In Trine 2 you could invest in skills for each hero, making them stronger in turn. Zoya would get freeze or fire arrows for example, Amadeus could conjure up to 3 or 4 boxes, and Amadeus got various combat skills, etc. All of that was scrapped. They also somehow thought that transitioning the game to 3D would be a great idea. It isn't. The camera is fixed, the 3D doesn't really add anything to the game, on the contrary, it makes it harder to navigate the levels without falling to your death. The controls in general don't help here. They're a mess, especially for Amadeus and Zoya. Zoya is also now almost completely useless in a fight compared to Pontius. Since there is no character progression at all in the game...no new mechanics, nothing, I was thankful it only took away 4 hours of my time. Of course the story is now completely open-ended and we would have been looking at at least 2 more Trine games to finish it...which might never happen (hopefully not, it's just milking the franchise with this one...and they got the red card for it I hope).

title: Trine 3: The Artifacts of Power
text: I rate the game Trine 3: The Artifacts of Power 2.5/5. Not good. Not terrible but not good either. Worse than mediocre. Almost bad. It's too bad but the third installment of the Trine series is a terrible letdown. It is a short game and features two key design decisions which were essentially bad ideas to begin with; The incorporation of 3 dimensional movement into the game and the requirement that you must collect a certain number of items (gold triangles or trine-angles) to unlock the next level. Simply making your way through an area isn't good enough anymore. These combine to make the game needlessly frustrating and needlessly repetitious and these critical flaws overwhelm what could have been a fun, though fairly short, third-person adventure-puzzle game experience. Good things: +The graphics of this game are very good (but are not as beautiful as the graphics in Trine 2, amazingly enough, despite the higher system requirements of this game). +The Voice acting is good. +The sound effects are good and crisp and clear. Mediocre things: +/-The puzzles are more simple in Trine 3 than the puzzles we have already been exposed to in Trine 1 and Trine 2. +/-The game is short (but I found myself wanting the game to be over because of the frustrating 3D elements of this game) +/-The music was largely mediocre. It fit the environments well but was also fairly forgettable. Bad Things: -The story ends with yet another classic stupid cliff-hanger computer game ending which pretty much advertises the idea of a Trine 4. Due to it's brevity, the game feels unfinished somehow. The story certainly isn't finished. -The between-stage game-board idea is an interesting concept but needing to gather trine-angles to unlock the next level results in needless repetition of levels and a frustrating and sometimes grinding experience which actually had me, in a way, glad that they game was so short. -The new 3D movement elements result in frustrating controls and imprecise jumps which often lead to your characters' deaths. The jumping mechanices remind me of those found in Supermario 64, except unlike in that game, in Trine 3 you cannot change the angle of the camera. As a result, trying to judge how far away another ledge is without the benefit of having any depth perception (since the game is on a flat computer monitor screen) is a very hit and miss, imprecise experience. To make matters worse, gathering enough Trine-angles to open up the latter and ending stages of the game requires you to gather these Trine-angles by solving exactly these kind of 3D jumping puzzles. It seems odd to say so in this day and age but this would have been a better game had it been in 2D (like in Trine 2) instead of 3D, -The game tries to spice up the pretty environments by having a whole large area devoted to running around inside the pages of a dusty book but the result is a large level in the middle of an otherwise fairly pretty game that is extremely ugly. -As usual for this series, this game features a lack of choice. You cannot make decisions which would change the plot or the game's ending or what levels you do or do not get to play.

title: Trine 3: The Artifacts of Power
text: I originally gave this game a negative review, and this was largely because I feel like, for the price, it is much too short (three or four hours of gameplay, depending on how long you spend messing around). However, upon playing it some more, and upon hearing from the developers why this game was so short (due to budget constraints, mostly), I've decided to give it, overall, a thumbs up. The gameplay is fun (there's just not enough of it), and it really is gorgeous. The mechanics are pretty nice (despite there being no upgrades, which I miss), and, since it exited early access, the bugs are very few and far between. The reason that I decided to change my review from a negative to a positive one is because I would like to see more of this game, which will only happen if the developers get the support they need. It would be stupid if a game which was criticised for being too short had to remain short only because it was criticised for it. They were (and hopefully, still are) planning to make more of this story, but they could only bring out so much to start with (which the marketers did NOT make clear in early access), hence the cliff hanger ending. It really is a nice concept. They've taken a 2D platforming game and turned it into a 3D one, which is still beautiful and still works well, and I, as a long time fan of the whole series, would really like to see some more of the Trine series made. I was a bit annoyed when it first came out about how much money I'd paid for such a short game, but it IS worth it to support the developers, and it IS a very good game.  7/10 (because there are no upgrades, but otherwise it's very nice to play)  9/10 (It IS beautiful. Fleeting, but beautiful.)  4/10 (4 hours and I would have liked 10)  6/10 (because it's too short and there are no upgrades to work towards, but if it was made longer this would definitely be an 8 or 9/10)

title: Two Digits
text: Overall, I'd have to say that I don't recommend this game.  It doesn't feel so much like a puzzle as it does math homework.  One of the worst features was the poorly organized difficulty and sense of progression.  Honestly, at the earlier part of the game, I felt like the solutions were harder to discover, though that probably had something to do with me working out the best manner of solving the puzzles in this game.  One of the best things a puzzle game of this nature can do is work up to harder puzzles so the player gets time to adjust to the sort of mindset they need to play the game and then become challenged the further they get.  However, several late-game puzzles were incredibly simplistic, especially the last set of puzzles with the multiples of 3.  It was not uncommon for me to merely add 2 or 3 numbers to match a number that was already listed in the puzzle, such as 5, 37, and 41 for 83. The strategy I found myself using in the game was not to add up the numbers to see what totals I'd get and try to find other numbers that were close to or equal to that sum.  Instead I looked at the numbers and would look for patterns in how much difference there was between the numbers.  For instance, say the 9 numbers listed were: 1, 7, 15, 20, 25, 28, 40, 49, and 71.  With a 1 and 7 on there, if I find two numbers that have either a gap of 1, 7, or 8 that will solve the puzzle.  15, 20, and 25 all have gaps of 5, but I can't make a 5 anywhere else.  What works though is taking 20 and 28 for 48, which is only 1 off from 49.  Adding up simpler numbers like that and looking for smaller increments and differences is much easier than trying to add up numbers that get into the hundreds. Much easier to realize that 73 and 75 are two apart, 41 and 42 are one apart, and 67 and 70 are three apart so you take the two smaller numbers from the one and two apart category and add it to the bigger number from the three apart to match the other set.  73+41+70=184 & 75+42+67=184  Not sure if that translates well typed out, but that style of thinking makes the puzzles much easier; at least it did for me. I played the game through for the achievements, but I've done my math homework.  I want to actually play some games now.

title: Two Digits
text: From what I've played so far, it's a very simplistic game, but that's not specifically why I wouldn't recommend it. 1. There are a LOT of levels. Normally, I'm not one to complain about too much content, but the additional levels do not add anything of value on top of normal game play. 250 levels is too many to justify individual selection and 'progress'. Levels should indicate a distinct progression: new mechanisms, bigger puzzles, etc. Levels here mean nothing in terms of playstyle. An example of what good level progression would be HexCells, where new worlds either introduce a new mechanic, or increase the difficulty of the puzzles. In Two Digits, the progression means nothing. 2. Poor PC porting. To anybody who has played this game or watched the trailers or screen shots, it's obvious this game was developed with touch screen in mind. If a game that is made on a different platform is ported to a new platform, the controls (or at least the options for controls) should reflect the new platform. In this case, it was minimally done. I see potential for left/right clicking to switch between states, but it was never addressed. In my opinion, calling this a puzzle is a bit of a stretch. At the very least, it has puzzle elements, but this plays more like a math education game than your standard puzzle. For an educational game, it wouldn't be that bad (I could see a style of this game being extended to other operations and potentially being a great tool for educators), but as a puzzle game on Steam, it might be hitting the wrong core demographic. The concept's not bad, but I think the execution could be better.
